articles.title: Vereadores pedem apuração sobre redução de ônibus no 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Comissão se reuniu com presidente da Casa durante a tarde desta terça-feira (27). Grupo quer responsabilizar envolvidos.
articles.summary: Comissão se reuniu com presidente da Casa durante a tarde desta terça-feira (27). Grupo quer responsabilizar envolvidos
articles.body:
Um grupo de vereadores de Salvador pediu, nesta terça-feira (27), a abertura de uma investigação na Câmara Municipal sobre redução da frota de ônibus na cidade durante o 2º turno das eleições , ocorrido no domingo (25).

A proposta foi apresentada ao presidente da Casa, vereador Carlos Muniz (PSDB), durante a tarde, em reunião a portas fechadas. O objetivo é responsabilizar os envolvidos, caso seja confirmado o erro.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, a oposição, que é minoria na Casa, tinha 10 das 14 assinaturas necessárias para a abertura da Comissão Especial de Inquérito (CEI). A Câmara de Salvador tem 43 vereadores.

"É colher essas assinaturas e fazer com que, se houver o acolhimento das 14 assinaturas, abrir essa CEI. Mais do que isso é esperar a investigação que está sendo feita pela Polícia Federal para que nós possamos tomar algum tipo de providência", destacou o presidente da Casa.

Ao menos 75 ônibus são impedidos de sair de garagens de Salvador durante o 2º turno das eleições — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Nesta terça-feira, a TV Bahia teve acesso ao processo que tramita no Tribunal Regional Eleitoral da Bahia (TRE-BA). No documento, os juízes relatam falhas encontradas durante vistoria nas garagens das empresas de ônibus.

Na sede do BRT, localizada na Avenida Barros Reis, as autoridades foram recebidas por um supervisor, que "confirmou que a frota que estava circulando era inferior à frota que circula durante a semana, e que a empresa segue orientação recebida da Semob".

Depois, os juízes foram até a sede da Integra Verde G2, no bairro de Santa Mônica, e constataram diversos veículos estacionados na garagem. No local, eles foram recebidos por um operador de tráfego, que também confirmou que a frota circulando era menor do que a frota semanal.

Por último, o grupo se dirigiu até a garagem da Ottrans G1, situada na Estrada Velha de Campinas de Pirajá, onde encontrou a mesma situação: ônibus parados e um operador de tráfego também confirmando que a frota circulando era menor do que a frota durante a semana.

A equipe de reportagem também teve acesso aos vídeos anexados ao processo que mostram as garagens com dezenas de ônibus parados. O Programa de Proteção e Defesa do Consumidor (Procon) também realizou fiscalização e diz que encontrou mais de 950 coletivos parados.

Em entrevista à TV Bahia nesta terça-feira, o secretário de mobilidade de Salvador (Semob), Pablo Souza, afirmou que a prefeitura adotou a mesma estratégia de transporte nos dois turnos de eleições e que o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) não determinou que 100% da frota de ônibus estivesse disponível em nenhuma cidade do país.

" Adotamos no domingo exatamente a mesma estratégia que adotamos no primeiro turno das eleições deste ano. Há mais de 10 anos, a prefeitura de Salvador adota a mesma estratégia. O TSE, em nenhum momento, determinou que 100% da frota de ônibus estivesse em nenhuma cidade do país", afirmou.

Em contrapartida, a resolução nº 23.751 do TSE, de fevereiro de 2026, diz que: "o poder público adotará as providências necessárias para assegurar, nos dias de votação, a oferta gratuita de transporte coletivo urbano municipal e intermunicipal, inclusive o metropolitano, com frequência compatível com aquela dos dias úteis (Supremo Tribunal Federal, ADPF nº 1.013/DF)".

Além disso, um texto veiculado no site da Semob, informa que a operação do segundo turno das eleições contaria com "100% da frota utilizada em dias úteis, sem a redução habitual de veículos aos domingos" . (Veja imagem abaixo)

Texto publicado no site da Secretaria de Mobilidade de Salvador antes do 2º turno de eleições — Foto: Redes sociais

O secretário de mobilidade afirmou que a frota de ônibus de Salvador é de 1,7 mil veículos, e que, no primeiro e no segundo turno, 850 veículos operaram nas ruas — ou seja, 50% da frota. Ele também informou que a prefeitura de Salvador usa a mesma operação de transporte em dias de eleições há 10 anos e nunca colocou 100% dos ônibus nas ruas.

O Sindicato dos Rodoviários de Salvador confirmou que, aos fins de semana, a frota é reduzida para até 50%, devido a folgas dos funcionários. No dia do segundo turno, a operação montada era de um domingo comum.

De acordo com o secretário, a única diferença entre a operação do primeiro e segundo turno está relacionada a colagem de adesivos com propaganda eleitoral nos coletivos . Imagens mostram que adesivos com o número 13, número da campanha de Lula (PT), foram colados nos ônibus que estavam nas garagens, o que é proibido.

Por causa disso, pelo menos 75 ônibus dos transporte público de Salvador foram impedidos de sair das garagens na manhã de domingo, informação que foi confirmada pela prefeitura. Em entrevista, o secretário afirmou que a operação foi regulada rapidamente , assim que a secretaria percebeu que a retirada dos adesivos estava atrapalhando o fluxo de transportes.

"Nossa equipe prontamente entrou no circuito. Praticamente toda a frota que estava na garagem neste dia amanheceu adesivada e as empresas de ônibus iniciaram logo cedo a remoção, que é determinada pela TSE. Quando a gente identificou que estava tendo impacto operacional, entramos no circuito e determinados que não impedissem nenhum ônibus sair da garagem", afirmou o secretário.

Secretário de Mobilidade de Salvador, Pablo Souza — Foto: TV Bahia

Drone flagrou ônibus parados nas garagens

O secretário também contou que as empresas dos ônibus adotaram a medida de retirar os adesivos com as equipes de limpeza, e não com o motorista de cada coletivo. Ele não informou quanto tempo levou entre o início da retirada dos adesivo e a liberação da frota .

Ainda segundo o secretário, o serviço já estava normalizado pela tarde. Apesar disso, vídeos mostram a mobilização de moradores com caronas solidárias . Diversos motoristas passaram nos pontos de ônibus para ajudar quem não conseguia chegar no local de votação devido a falta de ônibus.

O secretário e a prefeitura também não informaram o número total de ônibus impactados. Dois levantamentos foram divulgados ao longo do domingo:

➡️ Uma fiscalização da Polícia Federal (PF), feita em uma garagem da cidade, observou redução de 42,1% da frota , com 53 veículos a menos nas ruas, se comparado com a operação de um dia comum.

➡️ O Procon identificou 944 ônibus parados em garagens da OT Trans e Integra Plataforma.

O Secretário Pablo Souza estava em uma viagem de trabalho em Paris, na França, no domingo . Ao ser questionado sobre quem estava no comando da operação de mobilidade durante o segundo turno das eleições, ele afirmou que atuou no processo mesmo em outro país.

"Embora eu estivesse em uma missão institucional a convite do governo francês, nós fizemos a mesma programação do primeiro turno. E apesar de estar fora do país, atuei junto com toda a equipe, fiz contato com todos os empresários, com a direção e coordenação da secretaria de mobilidade e com o sindicato".

"Atuei de forma firme, para garantir que independente dessa divergência, os ônibus pudessem circular", afirmou.

Em meio a falta de ônibus no domingo, o TSE chegou a pedir a prisão em flagrante do secretário . Como ele não estava no Brasil no momento do pedido, ele não foi preso. Na segunda-feira (26), o próprio órgão revogou a prisão com a justificativa da perda da finalidade imediata da prisão devido ao encerramento da votação.

O cancelamento da ordem não significa absolvição nem reconhecimento de que não houve crime. A Justiça determinou que a Polícia Federal (PF) investigue o caso e deu 48 horas para que a prefeitura envie os documentos relacionados ao caso.

Segundo o secretário, a medida será atendida e os documentos serão enviados no prazo.

articles.title: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare
articles.summary: As the US president casts doubt on the security of the midterm elections, BBC Verify examines his claims.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud in the US which lead to a conviction.

Ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, Trump has been casting doubt on the security of the vote - alleging "rampant" cheating in postal voting and non-citizens voting.

However, studies suggest actual cases of these are extremely rare.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the evidence and Trump's proposed changes to the voting system.

How has Trump tried to change postal voting?

For years, Trump has made repeated unsubstantiated claims that postal voting leads to widespread fraud.

He has also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail in the midterms and has said he has cast his ballot by post in the past.

The president has been unsuccessful in his push for Congress to pass an act which would only allow people to vote by mail if they are disabled, ill, serving in the military, or travelling.

The majority of states allow people to vote by mail without having to provide a reason, and in the 2024 presidential election about 48 million people cast postal ballots.

Trump signed an executive order last year which directed the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on lists of citizens compiled by government agencies. It also sought to require states to use the same envelope style for postal votes.

However, the order was rejected by the US Supreme Court which called such changes so close to the midterm elections "arbitrary and capricious" - but said it could revisit the issue afterwards.

US states have different rules for verifying postal ballots, but every state matches certain voter information on the ballots against what they have on file to check they are eligible and most also conduct signature checks .

What does the evidence show on postal voting fraud?

Studies of multiple US elections suggest postal vote fraud has been extremely rare.

The Brookings Institute policy research think tank looked at the 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections and found an average of about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million postal votes.

The report used a database kept by the Heritage Foundation - a think tank which has been aligned with Trump in the past - which records cases of electoral fraud that have ended in a conviction.

We looked back in the database over the last 20 years and found it has tallied 325 convictions as a result of the fraudulent use of postal ballots.

A 2020 study by the American Statistical Association looked at cases of voter fraud in eight states which send postal ballots to all eligible voters and found no evidence that voting by mail increased the risk of voter fraud overall.

For example, according to the study, Oregon recorded 40 fraud cases between 2000 and 2020 having sent out more than 100 million postal ballots over that period.

How has Trump tried to change voter ID rules?

Trump has claimed non-citizen voting is widespread, and prior to the 2024 election he said Democrats were allowing millions of migrants into the US "so they can vote, vote, vote".

It is illegal for non-citizens to vote in US federal elections - punishments can include a prison sentence, a fine, and deportation.

The voting act the president has pushed Congress to pass would require voters to show a government-issued photo identification before they cast their ballots, as well as proof of citizenship when registering to vote and ongoing citizenship verification.

Critics have raised concerns that stricter voter ID requirements could harm voter turnout as people may not have a passport or the required government-issued photo ID.

"We don't have a national ID card that the government gives out, unlike a lot of countries. Drivers licence is most common but it doesn't identify your immigration status so the ID that most Americans carry around wouldn't be enough for you to vote," says Jonathan Diaz, a voting rights expert at the Campaign Legal Center.

A 2023 survey by the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice suggested that about 21.3 million voting-age American citizens, or about 9%, do not have documents proving citizenship readily available.

However, others argue that there has been no noticeable impact from existing voter ID laws.

"When scholars look at the effect of voter ID laws - either what the conservatives say on fraud or what progressive groups warn against about voter suppression - there doesn't seem to be a lot of proof that either has happened," says Walter Olson, an election expert at the conservative Cato Institute.

A number of largely Republican-run states have tightened voter ID requirements in the last couple of years. There have been 21 restrictive voting laws enacted since the 2024 election to establish stricter ID requirements, according to a study by the Brennan Center for Justice .

What does the evidence show on non-citizens voting?

Multiple studies show proven instances of non-citizens voting in past US elections have been very small.

The Heritage Foundation's database identified 24 cases of non-citizens being convicted for voting between 2005 and 2025.

A 2026 analysis by Reuters of non-citizen voting cases brought in federal courts found that over the last 30 years 129 people have been criminally charged and 73 of those cases resulted in a conviction.

"The fact that it's illegal for non-citizens to vote is a pretty strong deterrent in the first place as many worry about their immigration status and it would be an extremely risky move to vote," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institute.

"There's never been any evidence that there are many people who have done that, certainly not enough to influence an election."

What about non-citizens registered on voter rolls?

Trump has also pushed for states to use a federal database - the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save) database - to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens and remove them from voter rolls.

The tool has access to information about naturalised citizens and non-citizens who have contacted the federal government previously. It was launched in the 1980s to help government agencies verify individuals' eligibility for government benefits based on their immigration status.

Critics have questioned the reliability of using the data to remove people from voter rolls as they say it could be outdated and include people who have since become US citizens - but the US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration using it this way.

"Federal databases can be invaluable to states trying to update their voter rolls so long as their limitations are understood," says Olson. "So part of the Trump plan which requires the sharing of information is positive, even if the second part to require states to treat the database contents as reliable despite their continuing evident gaps and inaccuracies is bad."

The use of the programme by individual states is voluntary, and from those who have used it recently the number of non-citizens detected has been small.

In Georgia, after an audit of the state's voter rolls, 432 possible non-citizens were identified on its voter rolls over 30 years.

The Department of Homeland Security provided Nevada with a list of 185 names which it claimed identified non-citizens who had been improperly allowed to register to vote, but state officials found that they were all in fact citizens.

The White House has pointed to a case in New Jersey, where this summer a software glitch in the state's drivers licensing department registered about 6,600 non-citizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. State officials have said fewer than 400 cast ballots and they have all now been removed from the system.

The US Justice Department requested that California doesn't count 20,000 postal ballots ahead of the midterms from people it claims are "likely non-citizen registrants" - but that request has been rejected by an appeals court.

Out of that 20,000, it has charged 28 people who the department says are non-citizens who had illegally registered to vote.

articles.title: Mamdani under fire over NYC schools as critics say mayor is devoid of education agenda despite $38B budget
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani campaigned on progressive K-12 education reform, but advocates say the New York City mayor has produced few substantive changes.
articles.body: Ten months into New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s term, education advocates tell Fox News Digital that the democratic socialist mayor is falling short of delivering on the education promises he made during his campaign. "It's not good enough to be the TikTok mayor for 900,000 New York City public school students and their families," said David Bloomfield, former general counsel for the New York City Board of Education. "We need movement, not just words." Mamdani, who campaigned on a progressive education platform, was expected to make significant changes to the city's struggling public school system, but education advocates argue that his first 10 months in office have produced few substantive changes to K-12 education. MAMDANI'S EDUCATION PLAN'S 'LACK OF MERIT' COULD FUNDAMENTALLY CHANGE STUDENT OUTCOMES: GOP LEADER WARNS "Mayor Mamdani has not addressed education adequately," Bloomfield said. "Ten months into his administration, there is no real overwhelming education agenda or, particularly, regarding racial segregation or enrollment decline and school mergers … We're really hearing nothing out of the administration." "Most people who are involved in education advocacy and many parents are disappointed because they really expected a big shift from the last administration. Mamdani ran on a very progressive agenda overall, a kind of activist agenda, and yet we haven't seen many changes from the Adams administration in terms of K-12 education," said Class Size Matters founder Leonie Haimson. Bloomfield, a professor emeritus at Brooklyn College, argued that Mamdani's administration has yet to establish a comprehensive strategy for addressing declining enrollment, racial segregation, overcrowded classrooms and other issues facing the Big Apple’s public school system. MAMDANI TURNS ON NEW YORK CITY TEACHERS UNION WITH LAWSUIT BLOCKING PAY RAISES FOR EDUCATORS "[Mamdani] is continuing mayoral control of New York City public schools, but without a real agenda," Bloomfield told Fox News Digital. New York City’s public schools operate under mayoral control, giving Mamdani broad authority over the system and its leadership, including Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels. New York City has allocated a $38.6 billion budget to its public schools, which serve nearly one million students. The city spends 50% more per student than Los Angeles and Chicago, the country's other two largest school districts, according to a New York Post analysis. Bloomfield questioned whether the city is directing funding where it is most needed. He said funding continues to support schools with declining enrollment, while overcrowded campuses "bursting at the seams" struggle to accommodate their student populations. "Money will go a long way to solving the education problem in New York," said Bloomfield. "The problem, though, where does that money go? How is that money used?" STEVE MOORE, ED POZZUOLI: STOP FUNDING SCHOOL SYSTEMS. LET THE MONEY FOLLOW THE CHILD Haimson, a longtime education advocate who fights for smaller class sizes in New York City, criticized Mamdani's sudden loss of momentum on overcrowded classrooms. A New York state law, signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul and supported by Mamdani when he was a state assemblyman, requires New York City public schools to limit class sizes to between 20 and 25 students, depending on grade level. Mamdani has sought a two-year extension of the compliance deadline, which would push full implementation to 2030. "The one thing he was most enthusiastic about was lowering class sizes and complying with the class size law. And yet, as soon as he got elected, he decided he wanted an extension," Haimson told Fox News Digital. "I expected that they would come out with a real plan on how that space would be created, and they have not done so," she added. Haimson said Mamdani’s education agenda remains limited compared with his broader campaign platform, arguing that his approach to K-12 schools has largely mirrored that of his predecessor, former New York City Mayor Eric Adams. CHICAGO'S HALF-EMPTY SCHOOLS REVEAL A CRISIS CITY LEADERS REFUSE TO CONFRONT Bloomfield echoed Haimson’s argument, saying that unlike Adams and former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, Mamdani lacks a clear education agenda. "I think there's disappointment. People want change," he said. "Change is necessary, whether it's in terms of race … quality education, reading scores, math scores. There really is a need for improvement, and yet we're hearing nothing out of City Hall or the Department of Education." During his first six months in office, Adams issued 21 press releases related to K-12 education — including announcements about expanding the gifted and talented program and introducing dyslexia screening — compared with Mamdani's 11 releases during the corresponding period, according to an analysis by Chalkbeat. While Haimson credited Mamdani with launching the city’s first 2-K initiative, which expands early education and childcare to 2-year-olds through a partnership with Hochul, she said the administration has paid little attention to students older than five. POWERFUL TEACHERS' UNIONS SHARE STRIKING LINK WITH STATES STRUGGLING TO TEACH KIDS TO READ "He really hasn't taken much interest in anything that relates to education once the child turns 5 years old," she said. "And of course, there's many, many years of schooling that make a huge difference in a child's life after the age of 5." Both Haimson and Bloomfield told Fox News Digital that Mamdani and Samuels must make K-12 education a more prominent priority for the administration and develop a clearer strategy for addressing persistent challenges. "I'd like him … to pay more attention to K-12 education, because he did get mayoral control renewed, and it really is one of the top responsibilities of mayors in this city is to make sure that New York City kids are getting a good education," Haimson said. "We really need either the chancellor, Kamar Samuels, or the mayor himself to step up," Bloomfield added.
